intro: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John each tell the story of Jesus from where they stood. Here their accounts are woven together, event by event and in order, so you can follow the story, see how the accounts fit, and meet the One they are all about.

movements.title: The Word Becomes Flesh
movements.summary: His coming foretold, His birth, and the hidden years in Nazareth.
movements.intro: Before Jesus says a word in public, God keeps old promises. Angels speak to a priest, a young woman and a carpenter; the Son of God is born in David’s town; and for thirty years He grows up in an ordinary village, unknown to the world.
story: The story begins before the beginning. John tells us that the Word who was with God, and was God, became flesh and lived among us. Luke, writing carefully for a friend named Theophilus, starts in the temple, where the angel Gabriel promises an old priest, Zacharias, a son who will prepare the way for the Lord.

Six months later Gabriel comes to Mary in Nazareth: she will bear the Son of the Highest. An angel reassures Joseph in a dream, and the child is born in Bethlehem, the town of David, and laid in a manger. Shepherds hear the news from angels; old Simeon and Anna recognize Him in the temple; wise men from the East come to worship.

Herod’s jealousy drives the family to Egypt until it is safe to return. Then the curtain nearly closes. We see Jesus once at twelve, already at home in His Father’s house, and then only this: He grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

movements.title: Preparing the Way
movements.summary: John the Baptist, the baptism of Jesus, and the temptation.
movements.intro: A prophet’s voice breaks four centuries of silence. John calls Israel to repent, Jesus steps into the Jordan with sinners, the Father speaks from heaven, and the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to face the enemy alone.
story: Around AD 26, John the Baptist appears in the wilderness, dressed like Elijah and preaching repentance. Crowds pour out to the Jordan. Then Jesus comes from Nazareth and asks to be baptized. John protests, but Jesus insists, taking His place among the people He came to save.

As He comes up from the water, the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father says, “You are My beloved Son.” At once the Spirit leads Him into the wilderness. For forty days He fasts and is tempted by the devil, and where Israel once failed in the wilderness, Jesus answers every temptation with the word of God.

movements.title: First Days in Judea
movements.summary: The first disciples, water into wine, Nicodemus, the woman at the well.
movements.intro: Only John tells us about this first year. Jesus gathers His first followers, reveals His glory at a wedding, clears the temple at Passover, and talks one on one with a teacher of Israel and a Samaritan woman.
story: John the Baptist points to Jesus: “Behold the Lamb of God!” Andrew and John follow Him, Andrew brings his brother Simon, and Philip finds Nathanael. At a wedding in Cana, Jesus turns water into wine, the first of His signs, and His disciples believe in Him.

At the first Passover of His ministry, Jesus drives the money changers out of the temple. In Jerusalem, Nicodemus comes by night and hears that he must be born again. On the way back north, Jesus stops at a well in Samaria and offers living water to a woman with a broken past, and a whole town comes to believe He is the Savior of the world.

movements.title: The Great Galilean Ministry
movements.summary: Crowds, healings, the Sermon on the Mount, and the parables by the sea.
movements.intro: Jesus makes Capernaum His home and Galilee His field. He calls fishermen, heals the sick, forgives sinners, teaches with authority, and tells parables by the sea. The crowds grow, and so does the opposition.
movements.order_note: Matthew often groups miracles and teaching by theme, so the exact order of some Galilean events is uncertain.
story: After John is imprisoned, Jesus returns to Galilee announcing that the kingdom of God is at hand. His hometown, Nazareth, rejects Him, so He settles in Capernaum on the shore. He calls Peter, Andrew, James and John from their nets and Matthew from his tax booth.

News spreads fast. Jesus casts out demons, heals Peter’s mother-in-law, cleanses a leper, and forgives and heals a paralyzed man lowered through a roof. He heals on the Sabbath and claims to be its Lord, and the religious leaders begin to plot.

From a mountain He chooses twelve apostles and teaches the Sermon on the Mount. He raises a widow’s son, welcomes a sinful woman, calms a storm, frees a man possessed by many demons and raises a little girl. Then, after John the Baptist is killed, He feeds five thousand people with five loaves, walks on the sea, and declares, “I am the bread of life.” Many who wanted bread turn away.

movements.title: Training the Twelve
movements.summary: Jesus draws His disciples aside: Peter’s confession and the Transfiguration.
movements.intro: Jesus spends less time with the crowds and more with the Twelve. Near Caesarea Philippi, Peter confesses Him as the Christ; Jesus begins to speak plainly of the cross; and on a high mountain three disciples see His glory.
story: Jesus travels north and east, beyond Galilee, to Gentile regions: Tyre and Sidon, the Decapolis. A Gentile mother’s faith moves Him, a deaf man hears, and four thousand are fed. The disciples still struggle to understand.

At Caesarea Philippi He asks, “Who do you say that I am?” Peter answers, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” From then on, Jesus tells them He must suffer, die and rise again. Six days later He is transfigured before Peter, James and John, and the Father says, “Hear Him!” Back in Galilee He teaches them about humility and forgiveness, as the road to Jerusalem comes into view.

movements.title: The Road to Jerusalem
movements.summary: Judea and Perea, Lazarus raised, many parables, and the last journey.
movements.intro: Jesus has “steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem.” Much of this movement comes from Luke’s long travel section, rich with parables found nowhere else, and from John’s account of the feasts in Jerusalem. It ends at Jericho, a week before Passover, with the cross in plain view.
movements.order_note: Luke often groups this material by theme, so the exact order of some events here is uncertain.
story: At the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus teaches in the temple and cries out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink.” He calls Himself the light of the world, heals a man born blind, and says He is the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep.

On the journey He sends out seventy messengers and tells some of His best-known parables: the Good Samaritan, the lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son, the rich man and Lazarus, the Pharisee and the tax collector. At Bethany He raises Lazarus from the dead, and the council decides that Jesus must die.

The last stage passes through Perea and Jericho. Jesus blesses children, meets a rich young ruler, tells His disciples a third time that He will be killed and rise again, opens the eyes of blind Bartimaeus, and brings salvation to the house of Zacchaeus.

movements.title: The Final Week
movements.summary: Palm Sunday, the Upper Room, the trials, and the cross.
movements.intro: About a third of the Gospels covers these days. Jesus enters Jerusalem as King, cleanses the temple, answers every challenge, shares the Passover with His disciples, prays in Gethsemane, and is betrayed, tried and crucified.
story: Six days before Passover, Mary of Bethany anoints Jesus for His burial. On Sunday He rides into Jerusalem on a donkey as crowds shout, “Hosanna!” On Monday He clears the temple. On Tuesday He answers the leaders’ traps one by one, then sits on the Mount of Olives and tells His disciples about the temple’s fall and His return.

On Thursday evening He washes His disciples’ feet, gives them the bread and the cup, promises the Holy Spirit and prays for them. In Gethsemane He prays, “Not My will, but Yours, be done.” Judas betrays Him with a kiss.

Through the night and morning He stands before Annas, Caiaphas, the council, Pilate and Herod. Peter denies Him three times. Pilate hands Him over to be crucified. At Golgotha, Jesus prays for His enemies, promises paradise to a dying thief, and cries, “It is finished!” He is buried in a borrowed tomb, and the tomb is sealed and guarded.

movements.title: Risen and Reigning
movements.summary: The empty tomb, the appearances, the Great Commission, and the ascension.
movements.intro: Early on the first day of the week, the tomb is empty. Over forty days the risen Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene, to the women, to Peter, to two disciples on the road, to the Eleven, to more than five hundred, and to James, and then He ascends to the Father.
story: Before dawn on Sunday, women come with spices and find the stone rolled away. Angels announce, “He is not here, but is risen!” Peter and John run to the tomb and find the grave clothes lying there. Jesus Himself appears to Mary Magdalene in the garden and to the other women on the way.

That afternoon He walks with two disciples to Emmaus and opens the Scriptures to them. That evening He stands among the disciples in a locked room, and a week later He invites doubting Thomas to touch His wounds. By the Sea of Galilee He restores Peter over breakfast.

On a mountain in Galilee He sends His followers to make disciples of all nations, promising, “I am with you always.” After forty days He leads them out near Bethany, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven. They return to Jerusalem with great joy, waiting for the promised Spirit.

events.title: Why Luke Wrote His Gospel
events.summary: Luke tells Theophilus why he wrote: he has carefully traced the eyewitness accounts of Jesus so that Theophilus may be certain of what he was taught.

events.title: The Word Became Flesh
events.summary: John opens his Gospel before creation: the eternal Word, who is God and made all things, became flesh, lived among us and made the Father known.

events.title: The Family Line of Jesus
events.summary: Matthew and Luke trace Jesus’ family line: Matthew from Abraham through David’s royal sons to Joseph, Luke from Joseph back through David to Adam and God.

fit.q: Matthew and Luke give different names for most of Jesus’ ancestors between David and Joseph. Matthew says Joseph’s father was Jacob; Luke says Heli. How can both be right?
fit.short: Many think Luke gives Mary’s line and Matthew Joseph’s; others see both as Joseph’s, one natural and one legal. Views differ.

events.title: An Angel Promises John’s Birth
events.summary: In the temple, the angel Gabriel tells the aged priest Zacharias that his barren wife Elizabeth will bear a son, John, who will prepare the way for the Lord.

events.title: The Angel Comes to Mary
events.summary: In Nazareth, Gabriel tells the virgin Mary she will conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear Jesus, the Son of God, heir to David’s throne. Mary believes.

events.title: Mary Visits Elizabeth
events.summary: Mary hurries to Elizabeth, whose unborn son leaps at her greeting; Elizabeth blesses Mary as mother of her Lord, and Mary sings praise to God her Savior.

events.title: John the Baptist Is Born
events.summary: John is born to Elizabeth; when Zacharias writes, “His name is John,” his speech returns, and he prophesies God’s salvation and his son’s calling.

events.title: An Angel Speaks to Joseph
events.summary: Joseph plans to end his betrothal quietly, but an angel tells him Mary’s Child is from the Holy Spirit, so Joseph takes Mary home and names the Child Jesus.

events.title: Jesus Is Born in Bethlehem
events.summary: A census ordered by Caesar Augustus brings Joseph and Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger.

fit.q: Matthew places Jesus’ birth in the days of Herod, who died in 4 BC. Luke links it to a census taken while Quirinius governed Syria, and the best-known census under Quirinius came in AD 6. Can both be right?
fit.short: Luke knew the later census (Acts 5:37) and calls this one “first.” It may have preceded his, or Quirinius held an earlier role.

events.title: Angels Appear to the Shepherds
events.summary: An angel announces to shepherds near Bethlehem the birth of a Savior, Christ the Lord; heaven’s army praises God, and the shepherds find the Child and spread the news.

events.title: The Child Is Named Jesus
events.summary: On the eighth day Jesus is circumcised as the law requires and receives the name Jesus, the name the angel gave before He was conceived.

events.title: Simeon and Anna Meet the Child
events.summary: At Jesus’ presentation in the temple, aged Simeon takes Him in his arms and praises God for His salvation; the prophetess Anna speaks of Him to all awaiting redemption.

events.title: Wise Men Come to Worship
events.summary: Guided by a star, wise men from the East find the young Child Jesus in Bethlehem, worship Him and give Him gifts, while King Herod plots against Him.

events.title: The Flight to Egypt
events.summary: Warned in a dream, Joseph takes Jesus and Mary to Egypt by night, and Herod, enraged, kills the young boys of Bethlehem.

events.title: Home to Nazareth
events.summary: After Herod dies, God brings Jesus out of Egypt and guides Joseph away from Judea to Nazareth in Galilee, where the Child grows in wisdom and grace.

fit.q: Luke says that after the presentation in the temple, Joseph and Mary returned to Nazareth. Matthew tells of the wise men in Bethlehem and a flight to Egypt, and only then a move to Nazareth, which Joseph seems to choose after hearing about Archelaus. How do the two fit?
fit.short: Luke passes over the months in Bethlehem and Egypt; Matthew tells them, and explains why the family went home to Nazareth rather than Judea.

events.title: The Boy Jesus in the Temple
events.summary: At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple after Passover, and when His anxious parents find Him, He speaks of being about His Father’s business.

events.title: John the Baptist Prepares the Way
events.summary: John the Baptist preaches repentance in the wilderness, baptizes crowds in the Jordan, and points away from himself to the Mightier One who is coming.

fit.q: Asked, “Are you Elijah?” John answered, “I am not.” Yet Jesus later said of John, “he is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11:14). Which is right?
fit.short: John denied being Elijah returned in person; Jesus meant that John came in Elijah’s spirit and power, as the angel had promised.

fit.q: Matthew says John called the Pharisees and Sadducees a “Brood of vipers!” Luke says he said it to the multitudes. Whom did he address?
fit.short: The religious leaders were among the crowds. Luke reports the warning as all heard it; Matthew names those it most targeted.

events.title: Jesus Is Baptized
events.summary: Jesus is baptized by John in the Jordan; the Spirit descends on Him like a dove, and the Father declares Him His beloved Son.

fit.q: In Matthew, John recognizes Jesus and protests, “I need to be baptized by You.” In John’s Gospel, the Baptist says, “I did not know Him” until he saw the Spirit descend. Did he know Jesus or not?
fit.short: John sensed who Jesus was and protested; God’s promised sign, the Spirit descending and remaining, made him certain.

fit.q: Matthew records the voice as “This is My beloved Son.” Mark and Luke have “You are My beloved Son.” Which did the Father say?
fit.short: Mark and Luke give the words as spoken to Jesus; Matthew gives them as testimony about Him. The meaning is the same.

events.title: Jesus Is Tempted in the Wilderness
events.summary: Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, Jesus fasts forty days and defeats the devil’s three temptations by answering each one with the word of God.

fit.q: Matthew puts the temple temptation second and the mountain third. Luke reverses them. Which order is right?
fit.short: Matthew’s Greek marks a sequence; Luke’s does not, and he arranges the scenes to end at the Jerusalem temple, a theme of his Gospel.

events.title: The First Disciples Follow Jesus
events.summary: Pointed to Jesus by John the Baptist, Andrew and another disciple follow Him; then Simon, Philip and Nathanael come, and Jesus promises them greater things.

fit.q: John says Andrew, Simon and others began following Jesus near the Jordan. Matthew, Mark and Luke say Jesus called Simon, Andrew, James and John beside the Sea of Galilee, and they left their nets. Which was the first call?
fit.short: John tells of the first meeting near the Jordan; the other Gospels tell of the later call by the sea to leave everything.

events.title: Water Becomes Wine at Cana
events.summary: At a wedding in Cana, Jesus turns water from six large stone jars into the best wine of the feast, His first sign, and His disciples believe in Him.

events.title: A Short Stay in Capernaum
events.summary: After Cana, Jesus goes down to Capernaum with His mother, His brothers and His disciples, and they stay there only a few days.

events.title: Jesus Clears the Temple
events.summary: At Passover Jesus drives the merchants and money changers out of the temple and, asked for a sign, points to the temple of His body.

fit.q: John places this cleansing at the first Passover of Jesus’ ministry. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell of Jesus clearing the temple in His last week (event 128). Did He do it twice, or is this one event placed differently?
fit.short: Many think Jesus cleared the temple twice, at the start and end of His ministry; others think one cleansing is placed differently. Views differ.

events.title: Jesus and Nicodemus
events.summary: Nicodemus, a leading Pharisee, comes to Jesus by night, and Jesus tells him he must be born again and that God gave His Son so believers may live.

events.title: “He Must Increase”
events.summary: Jesus and His disciples baptize in Judea; when John’s disciples complain that all are going to Him, John rejoices: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

events.title: The Woman at the Well
events.summary: Resting at Jacob’s well, Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, offers her living water, reveals Himself as the Messiah, and many in her town believe.

events.title: Jesus Returns to Galilee
events.summary: After John the Baptist is imprisoned, Jesus returns to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, preaching that the kingdom of God is at hand.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark say Jesus went to Galilee after John was put in prison. But John says that while Jesus was baptizing in Judea, John “had not yet been thrown into prison” (John 3:24), and that Jesus left Judea because of the Pharisees. Do the accounts clash?
fit.short: John tells of months before the Baptist’s arrest; the others begin after it. Both reasons, the arrest and the Pharisees, shaped one journey.

events.title: A Nobleman’s Son Is Healed
events.summary: At Cana, a nobleman begs Jesus to come and heal his dying son in Capernaum; Jesus sends him home with a word, and the boy recovers at that very hour.

events.title: Rejected at Nazareth
events.summary: In the Nazareth synagogue, Jesus reads Isaiah’s promise and declares it fulfilled; when He speaks of God’s mercy to Gentiles, His hometown tries to throw Him off a cliff.

fit.q: Matthew 13:54–58 and Mark 6:1–6 also tell of Jesus rejected in His hometown, later in His ministry. Is Luke telling that same visit early, or did Nazareth reject Him twice?
fit.short: Many see two visits, Luke’s early and Matthew and Mark’s later; others think Luke placed one visit first. Views differ.

fit.q: Jesus says the heavens were shut “three years and six months” in Elijah’s day. But 1 Kings 18:1 says the word of the LORD came to Elijah “in the third year.” Which is it?
fit.short: Kings dates a moment “in the third year,” probably of Elijah’s stay in Zarephath; the whole drought lasted longer, as James 5:17 agrees.

events.title: “Follow Me”: Four Fishermen
events.summary: By the Sea of Galilee, Jesus fills Simon’s empty nets after a fruitless night and calls Simon, Andrew, James and John to follow Him and become fishers of men.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark tell of a short call by the shore. Luke tells of teaching from a boat, a miraculous catch and a call that follows it. Is this one call told two ways, or two stages of the same call?
fit.short: Either one call, which Luke tells in full, or two stages: a first call by the shore, then the catch that settled it.

events.title: A Demon Cast Out in the Synagogue
events.summary: On a Sabbath in Capernaum, Jesus teaches with authority in the synagogue and commands an unclean spirit to come out of a man, and His fame spreads.

events.title: Peter’s Mother-in-Law Healed
events.summary: Leaving the synagogue, Jesus enters Simon’s house, takes his feverish mother-in-law by the hand, and she rises at once and serves them.

events.title: Healing at Sunset
events.summary: At sunset, as the Sabbath ends, the whole town of Capernaum gathers at the door, and Jesus heals the sick and casts out demons, fulfilling Isaiah’s word.

fit.q: Mark says they brought all the sick and Jesus healed “many.” Matthew says they brought “many” and He healed “all.” Did some go home unhealed?
fit.short: “Many” means a great number, not a part. Luke says Jesus healed every one of those brought to Him.

events.title: A Leper Is Cleansed
events.summary: A leper kneels before Jesus and says, “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” Jesus touches him, cleanses him, and sends him to the priest.

events.title: A Paralyzed Man Through the Roof
events.summary: Four friends lower a paralyzed man through a roof, and Jesus forgives his sins, then heals him to prove He has the right to forgive.

fit.q: Mark says the men dug through the roof. Luke says they let the man down through the tiles. Which was it?
fit.short: Mark describes breaking through the roof; Luke speaks of tiles, a picture his Greek readers knew. Both describe opening the roof.

events.title: Jesus Calls Matthew
events.summary: Jesus calls Matthew, also called Levi, from his tax office, eats with tax collectors and sinners at his feast, and answers His critics: He came to call sinners.

fit.q: Matthew’s Gospel says Jesus called “a man named Matthew.” Mark and Luke tell the same call of a tax collector named Levi. Are these two different men?
fit.short: Levi and Matthew are one man with two names, like Simon Peter. Matthew’s Gospel calls him “Matthew the tax collector.”

events.title: Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
events.passover: “A feast of the Jews” · John 5:1 (possibly Passover)
events.summary: At the pool of Bethesda, Jesus heals a man ill for thirty-eight years on the Sabbath, then answers His accusers by claiming to work as His Father works.

events.title: Lord of the Sabbath
events.summary: When Pharisees accuse His hungry disciples of breaking the Sabbath in a grainfield, Jesus answers from Scripture and declares Himself Lord of the Sabbath.

fit.q: Mark says David ate the showbread “in the days of Abiathar the high priest.” But 1 Samuel 21 says the priest who gave him the bread was Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father. Did Mark get the name wrong?
fit.short: Mark may point to the Scripture passage about Abiathar, or to the time of Abiathar, Ahimelech’s son, who soon became David’s high priest.

events.title: A Withered Hand Restored
events.summary: On a Sabbath, with His critics watching to accuse Him, Jesus restores a man’s withered hand in the synagogue, and the Pharisees begin plotting His death.

fit.q: Who asked the question about the Sabbath? In Matthew the Pharisees ask Jesus. In Mark and Luke, Jesus asks them.
fit.short: The leaders asked their test question; Jesus answered with a question of His own. Matthew records theirs, Mark and Luke record His.

events.title: Jesus Chooses the Twelve
events.summary: After a night of prayer on a mountain, Jesus calls His disciples and chooses twelve of them to be with Him and to be sent out as apostles.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark name Thaddaeus among the Twelve. Luke and Acts have no Thaddaeus but list “Judas the son of James.” Do the lists disagree about who the Twelve were?
fit.short: Thaddaeus (also called Lebbaeus) and Judas the son of James are one man with more than one name, like Simon Peter or Levi Matthew.

events.title: The Beatitudes
events.summary: Jesus opens His great sermon by pronouncing God’s blessing on the poor in spirit, the mourning, the meek and the persecuted, and promising them the kingdom.

fit.q: Matthew’s sermon is given on a mountain and fills three chapters. Luke’s is given on “a level place,” is about a quarter as long, and includes woes. Are these the same sermon, and if so, why do they differ so much?
fit.short: Most likely one sermon: Matthew gives the fuller form, Luke a shorter one for Gentile readers, spoken on a level place on the mountain.

events.title: Salt and Light
events.summary: Jesus tells His disciples that they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world, and calls them to let their good works be seen.

events.title: Jesus and the Law
events.summary: Jesus declares that He came to fulfill the Law, then shows its true depth: anger, lust, broken promises and revenge judged at the heart, and love even for enemies.

events.title: Giving, Praying and Fasting in Secret
events.summary: Jesus warns against giving, praying and fasting to be seen by others, teaches His disciples the Lord’s Prayer, and points them to the Father who sees in secret.

events.title: Treasure, Worry and Judging Others
events.summary: Jesus calls His disciples to store treasure in heaven, to trust their Father instead of worrying, to stop judging others, and to ask God boldly.

events.title: Two Roads, Two Trees, Two Houses
events.summary: Jesus ends His sermon with a choice between two roads, two trees and two houses, and the crowds are astonished at the authority of His teaching.

events.title: The Centurion’s Great Faith
events.summary: In Capernaum a Gentile centurion asks Jesus to heal his dying servant with only a word, and Jesus marvels at his faith and heals the servant from a distance.

fit.q: Matthew says the centurion came to Jesus and spoke with Him. Luke says he sent elders and then friends, because he did not think himself worthy to come. Did he come or not?
fit.short: The centurion spoke through elders and friends. Matthew credits the words to the man who sent them; Luke shows the messengers.

events.title: A Widow’s Son Raised at Nain
events.summary: At the gate of Nain, Jesus meets a widow burying her only son, has compassion on her, and raises the young man to life with a word.

events.title: John the Baptist’s Question
events.summary: From prison, John the Baptist sends to ask whether Jesus is the Coming One; Jesus answers with His works, then honors John before the crowds.

events.title: A Sinful Woman Anoints Jesus
events.summary: At a Pharisee’s dinner, a sinful woman weeps over Jesus’ feet and anoints them; Jesus tells a story of two debtors and declares her sins forgiven.

fit.q: All four Gospels tell of a woman anointing Jesus, and in three of them the host is named Simon. Is Luke’s story the same event as the anointing at Bethany (Matthew 26, Mark 14, John 12)?
fit.short: Different times, places, hosts, women and complaints. Luke tells of an earlier anointing in Galilee, not Mary’s anointing at Bethany.

events.title: The Women Who Traveled with Jesus
events.summary: Jesus travels through the towns of Galilee preaching the kingdom, with the Twelve and several women He had healed, who support Him from their own means.

events.title: The Beelzebub Accusation
events.summary: When Jesus frees a blind and mute man, the leaders claim He casts out demons by Beelzebub; Jesus exposes the charge and warns of unforgivable blasphemy.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark set this controversy in Galilee, shortly before the parables by the sea. Luke tells it in chapter 11, during Jesus’ later travels. Did it happen once or twice?
fit.short: Either Luke grouped this teaching by subject, or Jesus answered the same charge, which came up often, on another occasion.

events.title: The Sign of Jonah
events.summary: When scribes and Pharisees demand a sign, Jesus refuses every sign but Jonah’s and warns that someone greater than Jonah and Solomon is standing before them.

fit.q: Luke places this teaching on Jesus’ later journey (Luke 11), in a different order, with the two examples reversed. Is this the same occasion as in Matthew?
fit.short: Jesus gave the sign of Jonah more than once (Matthew 16:4), and each writer arranges the sayings to make his point.

fit.q: Jesus said He would be “three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.” But He died on Friday afternoon and rose early on Sunday. How do these fit?
fit.short: Jews counted part of a day as a whole day. Jesus also said “the third day” and “after three days” for the same span.

events.title: Jesus’ True Family
events.summary: When His mother and brothers come asking for Him, Jesus points to His disciples and says that whoever does God’s will is His true family.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark tell this scene before the parable of the sower; Luke tells it after. Which order is right?
fit.short: Matthew says both scenes happened the same day. Luke places the family scene after the sower to link it with hearing and doing God’s word.

events.title: The Parable of the Sower
events.summary: From a boat, Jesus tells the parable of the sower, then explains to His disciples why He speaks in parables and what the four kinds of ground mean.

fit.q: Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables “because” the people do not see. Mark says He does it “so that” they may not see. Did Jesus use parables to explain or to hide?
fit.short: Parables reveal to the willing and conceal from the hardened. Matthew stresses the cause, the people’s closed eyes; Mark stresses the result.

events.title: The Wheat and the Tares
events.summary: Jesus tells of an enemy who sows weeds among a farmer’s wheat, and of an owner who lets both grow together until the harvest.

events.title: The Mustard Seed and the Leaven
events.summary: Jesus compares the kingdom to a tiny mustard seed that becomes a tree and to leaven hidden in flour until the whole batch rises.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark place these parables by the Sea of Galilee. Luke places them after a Sabbath healing in a synagogue, on Jesus’ later journey. Which setting is right?
fit.short: Jesus may have told these short parables more than once, or Luke placed them by theme after a later Sabbath healing.

events.title: The Wheat and the Tares Explained
events.summary: In the house, Jesus explains the parable of the tares: He sows the good seed, the devil sows the bad, and His angels will separate them at the end.

events.title: The Treasure, the Pearl and the Net
events.summary: Jesus compares the kingdom to hidden treasure, a priceless pearl and a dragnet, then likens His instructed disciples to a householder bringing out treasures new and old.

events.title: Jesus Calms the Storm
events.summary: Crossing the Sea of Galilee at evening, Jesus sleeps through a violent storm, then rebukes the wind and waves, and His terrified disciples ask who He is.

fit.q: Matthew tells the storm in chapter 8, long before the parables of chapter 13. Mark says it happened on the evening of the day of parables. Which is right?
fit.short: Matthew groups his miracles by theme in chapters 8–9; Mark gives the time, the evening after the parables.

fit.q: Did Jesus rebuke the disciples’ fear before He calmed the storm (Matthew) or after (Mark and Luke)? And which words did the disciples cry out?
fit.short: Several frightened men shouted different words. Jesus may have spoken about their faith both as He rose and after the calm.

events.title: The Demon-Possessed Man of the Gerasenes
events.summary: Across the lake, Jesus frees a man held by a legion of demons, lets them enter a herd of swine, and sends the man home as His witness.

fit.q: Matthew says two demon-possessed men met Jesus. Mark and Luke tell of one. How many were there?
fit.short: There were two. Mark and Luke tell the story of the one who spoke and later became a witness; Matthew counts both.

fit.q: The NKJV reads “Gergesenes” in Matthew and “Gadarenes” in Mark and Luke, and many modern translations read Gerasenes. Where did this happen?
fit.short: Gadara was the district’s main city; Gergesa (Kursi) a lakeside town. Copies vary among the similar names, but all point to the eastern shore.

events.title: Jairus’s Daughter and the Woman Who Touched Him
events.summary: On His way to heal Jairus’s dying daughter, Jesus stops for a woman who touched His garment, then raises the girl from the dead.

fit.q: In Matthew, the ruler says his daughter “has just died.” In Mark and Luke, he says she is dying, and only later do messengers report her death. Which is right?
fit.short: Matthew compresses the story, leaving out the messengers and putting the girl’s death into the father’s first words.

fit.q: Matthew says the ruler came “while He spoke these things,” that is, while Jesus was answering a question about fasting. Mark and Luke tell the fasting question much earlier. When did Jairus come?
fit.short: Either the fasting question came the same day Jesus returned across the lake, or the writers grouped these stories by theme.

events.title: Two Blind Men and a Mute Man Healed
events.summary: Two blind men follow Jesus calling Him Son of David, and He opens their eyes; then He frees a mute man, and the Pharisees credit the devil.

events.title: Rejected Again at Nazareth
events.summary: Jesus teaches in the Nazareth synagogue, but His hometown takes offense at the carpenter they knew, and He does few mighty works there because of their unbelief.

fit.q: Luke tells of Jesus being rejected in the Nazareth synagogue at the start of His ministry (Luke 4:16–30). Is this the same visit?
fit.short: Many think Jesus visited Nazareth twice, with different outcomes; others think Luke placed this one visit early as a preview.

events.title: The Twelve Sent Out
events.summary: Jesus gives the Twelve authority over demons and disease, sends them two by two through Galilee to preach, and prepares them for both welcome and persecution.

fit.q: Mark says the Twelve could take “a staff” and wear sandals. Matthew says “nor sandals, nor staffs,” and Luke says “neither staffs.” Did Jesus allow a staff or not?
fit.short: Matthew forbids acquiring new gear; Mark allows the staff and sandals they already had. No spares: travel light and trust God.

events.title: The Death of John the Baptist
events.summary: Herod hears of Jesus and fears John has risen; the Gospels then tell how Herod, trapped by a rash oath, had John beheaded in prison.

fit.q: Matthew says Herod wanted to put John to death but feared the people. Mark says it was Herodias who wanted John dead, while Herod feared John and protected him. Which was it?
fit.short: Herod was divided: at times he wanted John dead, yet he feared both the crowds (Matthew) and John himself (Mark).

events.title: Feeding the Five Thousand
events.summary: Jesus feeds about five thousand men, besides women and children, with a boy’s five loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered.

fit.q: Who first raised the problem of feeding the crowd: Jesus (John) or the disciples (Matthew, Mark and Luke)?
fit.short: Jesus tested Philip as the crowd arrived; later the Twelve urged Him to send them away. John records one exchange, the others another.

fit.q: Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida. But Mark says that afterward the disciples crossed “to the other side, to Bethsaida” (Mark 6:45). How can both be true?
fit.short: The feeding was near Bethsaida on the northeast shore. Either there were two towns named Bethsaida, or the boat’s course went toward it first.

events.title: Jesus Walks on the Water
events.summary: After praying alone through the evening, Jesus walks across the stormy sea to His disciples, lifts sinking Peter, and the wind ceases as He enters the boat.

fit.q: In Matthew the disciples worship Jesus and say, “Truly You are the Son of God.” In Mark they are amazed, but “their heart was hardened.” Did they understand or not?
fit.short: That night the disciples worshiped in awe (Matthew) yet still did not grasp what the loaves meant (Mark). Both were true.

events.title: “I Am the Bread of Life”
events.summary: In the Capernaum synagogue, Jesus tells the crowd He fed that He Himself is the bread of life, and many disciples turn away while the Twelve stay.

events.title: What Truly Defiles
events.summary: When Pharisees from Jerusalem fault His disciples for eating with unwashed hands, Jesus exposes their traditions and teaches that defilement comes from the heart.

events.title: A Gentile Mother’s Faith
events.place: The region of Tyre and Sidon
events.summary: In Gentile country near Tyre, Jesus tests a mother pleading for her demon-possessed daughter, praises her humble, persistent faith, and heals the girl from a distance.

fit.q: Was the woman a Canaanite (Matthew) or a Greek and a Syro-Phoenician (Mark)?
fit.short: Both are true. The Phoenicians descended from the Canaanites; Mark uses the Roman-era name, Matthew the biblical one.

events.title: A Deaf Man Hears
events.summary: Back by the Sea of Galilee in the Decapolis, Jesus heals crowds of sick people and, taking one deaf man aside, opens his ears and loosens his tongue.

events.title: Feeding the Four Thousand
events.summary: In the Decapolis, Jesus feeds four thousand men, besides women and children, who have stayed with Him three days, using seven loaves and a few small fish.

fit.q: This story is very like the feeding of the five thousand. Is it the same event told twice?
fit.short: Two events. Jesus Himself recalls both feedings, with different loaves, crowds and baskets (Mark 8:19–20).

events.title: The Pharisees Demand a Sign
events.summary: Back on the Galilean shore, Jesus refuses the Pharisees’ and Sadducees’ demand for a sign from heaven and points them to the sign of Jonah.

fit.q: Mark says “no sign shall be given to this generation.” Matthew says no sign “except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” Did Jesus refuse a sign or promise one?
fit.short: Jesus refused a sign on demand (Mark). Matthew adds the one exception, the sign of Jonah: His death and resurrection.

fit.q: Matthew says they came to Magdala; Mark says Dalmanutha. Which was it?
fit.short: Dalmanutha was probably a village or landing place near Magdala. The two writers name the same district differently.

events.title: Beware the Leaven of the Pharisees
events.summary: Crossing the Sea of Galilee, Jesus warns His disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees, and they think He is talking about the bread they forgot.

fit.q: Matthew’s warning names the Sadducees; Mark’s names Herod. Which did Jesus say?
fit.short: Jesus may have named all three groups, or Matthew and Mark name one circle of opponents by its religious and political labels.

events.title: A Blind Man Healed in Two Stages
events.summary: At Bethsaida, Jesus leads a blind man out of the town and heals him in two stages: first blurred sight, then full and clear.

events.title: “You Are the Christ”
events.summary: Near Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks His disciples who they say He is, and Peter answers, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

fit.q: Jesus says, “you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church.” Is the rock Peter, Peter’s confession, or Christ Himself?
fit.short: Peter as first confessor and leader, Peter’s confession, or Christ Himself. Views differ; all agree Christ builds the church.

events.title: Jesus Foretells His Death
events.summary: From Caesarea Philippi on, Jesus teaches plainly that He must suffer, die and rise; He rebukes Peter and calls all who follow Him to take up their cross.

fit.q: Did Jesus say He would rise “after three days” (Mark) or “the third day” (Matthew and Luke)?
fit.short: Jews counted part of a day as a day. Even Jesus’ enemies used “after three days” and “the third day” for the same span.

fit.q: Jesus said some standing there would not die before they saw the kingdom come with power. They all died long ago. What did He mean?
fit.short: Many see the Transfiguration; others the resurrection and Pentecost, or the fall of Jerusalem. Each came within His hearers’ lifetime.

events.title: The Transfiguration
events.summary: On a high mountain, Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James and John, Moses and Elijah talk with Him, and the Father speaks from a cloud.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark say the Transfiguration came “after six days.” Luke says “about eight days.” Which is it?
fit.short: Matthew and Mark count the six days between; Luke gives a rough count, “about eight days,” that includes the first and last days.

events.title: A Boy Set Free
events.summary: Coming down the mountain, Jesus finds His disciples unable to free a boy from a violent spirit; He answers the father’s honest cry and sets the boy free.

fit.q: Why could the disciples not cast the spirit out? Matthew says it was their unbelief; Mark says this kind comes out only by prayer.
fit.short: Unbelief was the root; prayer was the remedy. Matthew and Mark record two sides of one private answer.

events.title: Jesus Foretells His Death a Second Time
events.summary: Passing quietly through Galilee, Jesus tells His disciples again that He will be betrayed, killed and raised; they do not understand and are afraid to ask.

events.title: A Coin in the Fish’s Mouth
events.summary: In Capernaum, collectors ask whether Jesus pays the temple tax; He teaches Peter that the King’s Son is free, then pays it with a coin from a fish.

events.title: Who Is the Greatest?
events.summary: Back in Capernaum, Jesus answers His disciples’ argument about greatness by setting a little child among them and warning against causing any little one to stumble.

fit.q: Did Jesus raise the question of greatness (Mark and Luke), or did the disciples bring it to Him (Matthew)?
fit.short: Jesus asked what they had argued about; they fell silent, then asked Him openly. The Gospels record different moments of one conversation.

events.title: Forgiveness and the Unforgiving Servant
events.summary: Jesus teaches how to win back a brother who sins, then answers Peter’s question about forgiving with a parable of a servant forgiven a debt beyond paying.

events.title: At the Feast of Tabernacles
events.summary: At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus goes up quietly, then teaches openly in the temple, invites the thirsty to come to Him, and divides both crowd and council.

fit.q: Jesus told His brothers, “I am not yet going up to this feast,” and then went up after they left. Did He change His mind or mislead them?
fit.short: Jesus refused His brothers’ plan of a public display. He went up later, quietly, on the Father’s timing rather than theirs.

events.title: A Woman Caught in Adultery
events.summary: Scribes and Pharisees bring Jesus a woman caught in adultery to trap Him; He turns the question on their consciences and sends her away uncondemned, to sin no more.

events.title: “I Am the Light of the World”
events.summary: In the temple, Jesus calls Himself the light of the world and finally says, “Before Abraham was, I AM,” and His hearers take up stones.

events.title: The Seventy Sent Out
events.summary: Jesus sends seventy disciples ahead of Him two by two. They return rejoicing that demons obeyed them; He points them to a greater joy: names written in heaven.

events.title: The Good Samaritan
events.summary: A lawyer asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life, then who his neighbor is. Jesus answers with a story of a Samaritan who stops to save a wounded stranger.

events.title: Mary and Martha
events.summary: In Martha’s home, Jesus defends Mary for sitting at His feet while Martha frets over serving: Mary has chosen the one thing needed.

events.title: A Man Born Blind Receives His Sight
events.summary: On a Sabbath Jesus gives sight to a man born blind; the Pharisees throw the man out, but Jesus finds him, and he believes and worships.

events.title: The Good Shepherd
events.summary: Jesus calls Himself the door of the sheep and the good shepherd who lays down His life and takes it up again, and the crowd divides over Him.

events.title: At the Feast of Dedication
events.summary: At the Feast of Dedication, Jesus says His sheep are safe in His and the Father’s hands and declares, “I and My Father are one.” They take up stones.

events.title: Withdrawing Beyond the Jordan
events.summary: Jesus withdraws beyond the Jordan to the place where John first baptized, and many come to Him and believe, saying all John said about Him was true.

events.title: Lazarus Raised from the Dead
events.summary: Jesus comes to Bethany when Lazarus has been dead four days, weeps with the mourners, and calls him out of the tomb: He is the resurrection and the life.

events.title: The Council Plots His Death
events.summary: Alarmed by the raising of Lazarus, the council plots Jesus’ death; Caiaphas says one man should die for the people, and Jesus withdraws to Ephraim.

events.title: Setting Out for Jerusalem
events.summary: Jesus leaves Galilee and resolutely sets out for Jerusalem; He rebukes James and John for wanting fire on a Samaritan village and tells would-be followers the cost.

fit.q: Luke places the would-be followers at the start of Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem. Matthew sets two of the same conversations much earlier, by the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 8:19–22). When did they happen?
fit.short: Luke arranges his journey loosely, without dates. Matthew may place the same conversation differently, or Jesus had a similar one on another day.

fit.q: Luke has Jesus heading into Samaria. Matthew and Mark say He came to Judea beyond the Jordan, east of the river. Which way did He go?
fit.short: Refused by a Samaritan village, Jesus went another way. Matthew and Mark tell where the road led: Judea beyond the Jordan.

events.title: Ten Lepers Cleansed
events.summary: On the border of Samaria and Galilee, Jesus cleanses ten lepers with a word; only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank Him.

events.title: “Lord, Teach Us to Pray”
events.summary: Asked to teach His disciples to pray, Jesus gives them a model prayer, a story of a request at midnight, and the promise of the Father’s best gift.

events.title: Woes to the Pharisees and Lawyers
events.summary: When His Pharisee host is surprised that He skipped the ritual washing, Jesus pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers for clean outsides and neglected hearts.

events.title: Beware of Hypocrisy and Greed
events.summary: Before a huge crowd, Jesus warns His disciples against hypocrisy and greed, tells of a rich fool, and calls them to fear God and trust their Father.

events.title: Be Ready
events.summary: Jesus calls His disciples to be ready and faithful like servants awaiting their master, speaks of the fire and division He brings, and urges the crowds to read the times.

events.title: Repent or Perish
events.summary: Told of Galileans killed by Pilate at their sacrifices, Jesus calls His hearers to repent, and tells of a barren fig tree given one more year.

events.title: A Bent Woman Set Free on the Sabbath
events.summary: Teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus frees a woman who has been bent over for eighteen years, and answers the indignant synagogue ruler.

events.title: The Narrow Door
events.summary: Asked whether few are saved, Jesus urges His hearers to strive to enter the narrow door, sends a reply to Herod, and laments over Jerusalem.

events.title: At a Pharisee’s Table: The Great Supper
events.summary: At a Sabbath meal in a leading Pharisee’s house, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, teaches about seats and guest lists, and tells the parable of the great supper.

events.title: The Cost of Following Jesus
events.summary: Turning to the great crowds traveling with Him, Jesus tells them that following Him costs everything and urges them to count the cost before they begin.

events.title: Lost Sheep, Lost Coin, Lost Son
events.summary: Jesus answers complaints that He welcomes sinners with three parables of lost things found, ending with an older brother who refuses to join the feast.

events.title: The Shrewd Steward
events.summary: Jesus tells of a steward, about to lose his post, who wins friends by reducing his master’s debtors’ bills, and teaches His disciples faithfulness with money.

events.title: The Rich Man and Lazarus
events.summary: When Pharisees who loved money scoff at Him, Jesus tells of a rich man and a beggar named Lazarus whose places are reversed after death.

events.title: Faith, Forgiveness and Duty
events.summary: Jesus warns His disciples against causing others to stumble, commands them to forgive again and again, answers their plea for more faith, and teaches that servants simply do their duty.

events.title: When the Kingdom Comes
events.summary: Asked by Pharisees when God’s kingdom will come, Jesus says it does not come with signs to watch for, then warns His disciples that His day will come suddenly.

fit.q: Much of this teaching, the lightning, the days of Noah, the housetop and the field, one taken and the other left, appears again in Matthew 24, in Jesus’ last discourse on the Mount of Olives. Did Luke move it, or did Jesus say it twice?
fit.short: Jesus gave these warnings on the road (Luke 17) and again on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24). Luke himself records both occasions.

events.title: The Persistent Widow
events.summary: Jesus tells of a widow who kept coming to an unjust judge until he gave her justice, to teach that His people should always pray and not lose heart.

events.title: The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
events.summary: Jesus contrasts a Pharisee who prayed about his own goodness with a tax collector who begged for mercy, and says the tax collector went home justified.

events.title: A Question About Divorce
events.summary: Pharisees test Jesus with a question about divorce, and He takes them back to creation, where God made husband and wife one flesh.

fit.q: Mark records Jesus’ words with no exception: whoever divorces and remarries commits adultery. Matthew includes “except for sexual immorality.” Did Jesus allow an exception or not?
fit.short: Matthew records the exception Jesus gave to the Pharisees’ question; Mark states the general rule. Both teach that God intends marriage to last.

fit.q: If the exception is part of Jesus’ teaching, how far does it reach? Does it allow divorce only, or remarriage too?
fit.short: Many evangelicals see unfaithfulness as a ground for divorce and remarriage; others allow divorce without remarriage, or read the exception more narrowly.

events.title: Jesus Blesses the Children
events.summary: When the disciples turn away people bringing children, Jesus is displeased, welcomes the children, takes them in His arms and blesses them.

events.title: The Rich Young Ruler
events.summary: A rich young ruler asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life, but goes away sorrowful when Jesus tells him to sell everything and follow Him.

fit.q: In the NKJV, Matthew agrees with Mark and Luke: the man says “Good Teacher,” and Jesus asks, “Why do you call Me good?” But many modern translations follow older manuscripts of Matthew, where the man says only Teacher and Jesus asks why he is asking Him about what is good. Did Jesus question the title or the question?
fit.short: The man spoke of a good Teacher and a good deed. Jesus answered both: only God is good. The Gospels record different parts of one reply.

events.title: The Workers in the Vineyard
events.summary: Jesus tells of a landowner who pays workers hired at the end of the day the same wage as those who worked all day, picturing the generosity of God’s kingdom.

events.title: Jesus Foretells His Death a Third Time
events.summary: On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus tells the Twelve in detail that He will be betrayed, condemned, mocked, scourged, killed and raised the third day.

events.title: James and John Ask for Thrones
events.summary: James and John, with their mother, ask Jesus for the places at His right and left; He speaks of His cup and teaches that greatness means serving.

fit.q: Matthew says the mother of James and John asked for the seats. Mark says the brothers asked. Who made the request?
fit.short: She came with her sons and spoke for them; in both Gospels Jesus answers the brothers. Mark tells the request as theirs.

events.title: Blind Bartimaeus Receives His Sight
events.summary: On His last journey to Jerusalem, Jesus stops for a blind beggar the crowd wanted silenced, and gives him his sight.

fit.q: Was there one blind man or two? And did the healing happen as Jesus was leaving Jericho or as He was coming near it?
fit.short: Mark and Luke name the man the church knew; Matthew counts both. There were two Jerichos, old and new.

events.title: Zacchaeus Comes Down
events.summary: In Jericho, Jesus calls a rich chief tax collector down from a sycamore tree, stays at his house, and declares that salvation has come to it.

events.title: The Parable of the Minas
events.summary: Near Jerusalem, with the crowd expecting the kingdom at once, Jesus tells of a nobleman who leaves to receive a kingdom and returns to judge his servants and his enemies.

fit.q: Luke’s parable of the minas is much like Matthew’s parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30). Is it one parable remembered two different ways?
fit.short: Two parables on two occasions: the minas near Jericho to a crowd, the talents on the Mount of Olives to the disciples, with different details.

events.title: Jesus Arrives at Bethany
events.summary: With Passover near and an order out for His arrest, Jesus comes to Bethany six days before the feast, to the village where He raised Lazarus.

events.title: Mary Anoints Jesus
events.summary: At a supper in Bethany, Mary pours costly perfume on Jesus. Judas and others call it waste, but Jesus defends her and calls it an anointing for His burial.

fit.q: John places the anointing just after Jesus reached Bethany six days before Passover, on the night before the Triumphal Entry. Matthew and Mark tell it after saying Passover was two days away. When did it happen?
fit.short: John ties it to Jesus’ arrival six days before Passover. Matthew and Mark place the undated supper beside Judas’s bargain, which it helps explain.

fit.q: Did Mary anoint Jesus’ head (Matthew, Mark) or His feet (John)? And who complained: Judas (John), the disciples (Matthew) or “some” (Mark)?
fit.short: She anointed both head and feet. Judas started the complaint and other disciples joined in.

events.title: The Triumphal Entry
events.summary: Riding a colt down the Mount of Olives, Jesus enters Jerusalem as crowds spread cloaks and branches and shout “Hosanna!”, and He weeps over the city.

fit.q: Matthew says the disciples brought a donkey and a colt and set Jesus “on them” (21:7). Mark, Luke and John mention only a colt. Was there one animal or two?
fit.short: The colt’s mother came too. Matthew mentions both animals; the others mention only the colt Jesus rode.

events.title: The Fig Tree Cursed
events.summary: On the road from Bethany, Jesus is hungry, finds a fig tree in full leaf but without fruit, and declares that no one will eat from it again.

fit.q: Matthew says the fig tree withered immediately and goes straight on to the disciples’ amazement. Mark says they found it withered the next morning. Which is it?
fit.short: The tree began to wither at Jesus’ word; the disciples noticed the next morning. Matthew tells the cursing and the discovery as one story.

events.title: Jesus Clears the Temple in the Final Week
events.summary: Jesus drives the traders out of the temple, calls it a house of prayer made a den of thieves, heals the blind and lame there, and welcomes children’s praise.

fit.q: Did Jesus clear the temple on the day He rode into Jerusalem (Matthew, Luke) or the next day (Mark)?
fit.short: Mark gives the timing: Jesus looked around on Sunday and cleared the temple Monday. Matthew and Luke join the two scenes without a time note.

events.title: The Withered Fig Tree and Faith
events.summary: Passing the fig tree withered from the roots, Jesus tells His amazed disciples to have faith in God, to pray believing, and to forgive when they pray.

events.title: “By What Authority?”
events.summary: In the temple, the chief priests, scribes and elders demand to know by what authority Jesus acts. He asks them about John’s baptism, and they refuse to answer.

events.title: The Two Sons and the Wicked Tenants
events.summary: Jesus tells the temple leaders of two sons, one who refused but went, and of tenants who kill the owner’s son. The leaders see He means them.

fit.q: Who said the owner would destroy the tenants? In Matthew the listeners say it (21:41). In Mark and Luke, Jesus says it, and in Luke the people answer, “Certainly not!” (20:16).
fit.short: Listeners gave the verdict, Jesus confirmed it in His own words, and others in the crowd, seeing the point, cried “Certainly not!”

events.title: The Wedding Feast
events.summary: Jesus tells of a king whose invited guests refuse his son’s wedding feast, who fills the hall from the highways, and who expels a guest without a wedding garment.

fit.q: Luke tells a parable of a great supper whose invited guests make excuses, so the host brings in the poor and the outsiders (Luke 14:16–24). Is Matthew’s wedding feast the same parable?
fit.short: Different settings and different stories. Jesus told the great supper earlier and the wedding feast in the temple in His last week.

events.title: Taxes to Caesar and the Resurrection Question
events.summary: In the temple Jesus answers two traps: Pharisees and Herodians ask about taxes to Caesar, and Sadducees mock the resurrection with a riddle about seven brothers.

events.title: The Greatest Commandment
events.summary: Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus names love for God with all one’s being and love for neighbor, and tells an agreeing scribe he is not far from the kingdom.

fit.q: In Matthew a lawyer asks the question “testing Him.” In Mark a scribe asks because he sees Jesus has answered well, and Jesus praises his wise reply. Was the man hostile or friendly?
fit.short: The lawyer was a scribe. He came to test Jesus on the Pharisees’ behalf, and Mark shows him won over by the answer.

events.title: Whose Son Is the Christ?
events.summary: After a day of questions, Jesus asks one: how can the Christ be David’s Son when David, in Psalm 110, calls Him “Lord”? No one can answer.

events.title: Woes on the Scribes and Pharisees
events.summary: In the temple courts, Jesus warns the crowds and His disciples against the scribes and Pharisees, pronounces woes on their hypocrisy, and laments over Jerusalem.

fit.q: Matthew sets the lament “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem” in the temple during Jesus’ last week. Luke gives almost the same words earlier, on the journey to Jerusalem (Luke 13:34–35). When did Jesus say it?
fit.short: Jesus likely lamented over Jerusalem more than once: on the journey (Luke) and again in the temple after His entry (Matthew).

fit.q: Matthew calls the murdered Zechariah “son of Berechiah.” But the Zechariah stoned in the temple court was “the son of Jehoiada” (2 Chronicles 24:20–22), and “Zechariah the son of Berechiah” was the prophet (Zechariah 1:1). Whom did Jesus mean?
fit.short: Most think Jesus meant the Zechariah stoned in the temple court, the Hebrew Bible’s last martyr; “son of” can mean grandson.

events.title: The Widow’s Two Mites
events.summary: Sitting opposite the temple treasury, Jesus watches a poor widow drop in two tiny coins and tells His disciples she has given more than all the rich.

events.title: Greeks Ask to See Jesus
events.summary: When Greeks ask to see Him, Jesus announces that His hour has come, speaks of the grain that must die, and is answered by a voice from heaven.

events.title: The Olivet Discourse
events.summary: Leaving the temple for the last time, Jesus foretells its destruction and His own return, and calls His disciples to watch, endure and be ready.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark say the sign is “the abomination of desolation.” Luke says it is “Jerusalem surrounded by armies.” Did Jesus give two different signs?
fit.short: Luke explains Daniel’s phrase for Gentile readers: the sign would be Jerusalem surrounded by armies.

fit.q: Jesus said, “This generation will by no means pass away till all these things take place” (Matthew 24:34). Was He wrong about the timing of His coming?
fit.short: Many see the temple’s fall in AD 70, within a generation; others see a near event previewing the final one. Views differ.

events.title: The Plot and Judas’s Bargain
events.summary: Two days before Passover, Jesus foretells His betrayal; the chief priests plot to seize Him quietly, and Judas Iscariot agrees to hand Him over for money.

events.title: Preparing the Passover
events.summary: On the day the Passover lambs are killed, Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the meal in a large upper room, then sits down with the Twelve.

fit.q: Matthew, Mark and Luke call this meal the Passover, eaten on the day the lambs were killed. But John says that on Friday morning the priests would not enter Pilate’s headquarters, “that they might eat the Passover” (John 18:28), and calls Friday “the Preparation Day of the Passover” (John 19:14). Was the Last Supper a Passover meal?
fit.short: Many see a Thursday Passover, with John’s “Passover” meaning the whole feast; others propose two calendars or an early meal. Views differ.

events.title: Jesus Washes the Disciples’ Feet
events.summary: At supper on His last night, Jesus rises, ties a towel around Himself and washes His disciples’ feet, then tells them to follow His example.

events.title: The Betrayer Revealed
events.summary: At the table Jesus announces that one of the Twelve will betray Him; He quietly identifies Judas with a piece of bread, and Judas goes out into the night.

fit.q: Was Judas still at the table for the Lord’s Supper? Matthew and Mark tell of the betrayer before the bread and cup, and John says Judas left right after the piece of bread. Luke records Jesus’ words about the betrayer after the cup.
fit.short: Many think Judas left before the bread and cup; others follow Luke’s order and think he stayed. The text does not settle it.

fit.q: Luke says Satan entered Judas before he made his bargain with the chief priests (Luke 22:3). John says Satan entered him at the supper, after the piece of bread (John 13:27). Which is right?
fit.short: Satan prompted Judas before the bargain and took full hold of him at the supper. John himself shows both steps (13:2, 27).

events.title: The Lord’s Supper
events.summary: At the Passover table, Jesus gives the bread as His body and the cup as the new covenant in His blood, and commands, “do this in remembrance of Me.”

fit.q: Matthew and Mark place Jesus’ vow not to drink “of the fruit of the vine” again after the cup of the Supper. Luke places a similar vow before the bread (Luke 22:17–18). When did Jesus say it?
fit.short: Luke records two cups. Jesus likely spoke the vow with the first and repeated it with the last, or Luke arranged it by theme.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark record, “This is My blood of the new covenant.” Luke and Paul record, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood.” What exactly did Jesus say?
fit.short: Both forms say the same thing: the cup is His blood, which makes the new covenant. The Gospels give the sense faithfully.

events.title: A New Commandment; Peter Warned
events.summary: After Judas leaves, Jesus gives His disciples a new commandment to love as He has loved, and warns Peter that he will deny Him three times.

fit.q: Luke and John place Jesus’ warning to Peter in the upper room. Matthew and Mark place it after they sang a hymn and went out toward the Mount of Olives. Where was Peter warned?
fit.short: Jesus likely warned Peter at the table (Luke, John) and again on the way to the Mount of Olives (Matthew, Mark).

events.title: “I Am the Way”
events.summary: Jesus comforts His troubled disciples: He goes to prepare a place for them, He is the way to the Father, and He promises the Helper and His peace.

events.title: The Vine and the Branches
events.place: On the way to the garden
events.summary: Jesus calls Himself the true vine and His disciples the branches, urges them to abide in Him and love one another, and warns that the world will hate them.

events.title: The Promise of the Holy Spirit
events.place: On the way to the garden
events.summary: Jesus warns of coming persecution, promises that the Helper will come when He goes, and tells His grieving disciples that their sorrow will turn to joy.

events.title: Jesus Prays for His Own
events.summary: Before crossing the Kidron, Jesus lifts His eyes to heaven and prays for His own glory, for the eleven He is leaving, and for all who will believe through them.

events.title: Gethsemane
events.summary: In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prays in deep anguish that the cup might pass from Him, yields to His Father’s will, and finds His disciples asleep.

fit.q: The Gospels give the words of Jesus’ prayer in three slightly different forms. Which words did He actually pray?
fit.short: Jesus prayed at length, three times. Each Gospel gives the heart of it: take this cup away, yet Your will be done.

events.title: Betrayed and Arrested
events.summary: Judas leads an armed crowd to Gethsemane and betrays Jesus with a kiss; Jesus gives Himself up, heals a wounded servant, and His disciples flee.

fit.q: Why did Judas need to identify Jesus with a kiss if Jesus stepped forward and said, “I am He”? Which came first?
fit.short: No Gospel gives the order. Judas may have kissed Jesus on arrival before Jesus stepped forward, or the reverse. Either order fits.

events.title: Before Annas
events.summary: Bound, Jesus is taken first to Annas, the former high priest, who questions Him about His disciples and teaching; Jesus answers openly and is struck.

events.title: Before Caiaphas and the Council
events.summary: At night before Caiaphas and the council, false witnesses fail, Jesus declares under oath that He is the Christ, and He is condemned as deserving death.

fit.q: Did Jesus answer the high priest, “I am” (Mark) or “It is as you said” (Matthew)?
fit.short: “It is as you said” was a firm yes. Mark gives its plain sense, “I am”; the high priest heard it as a clear claim.

events.title: Peter Denies Jesus Three Times
events.summary: In the high priest’s courtyard, Peter three times denies knowing Jesus; the rooster crows, the Lord looks at him, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly.

fit.q: The Gospels differ over who challenged Peter and where: a girl at the door or by the fire, then another girl, the same girl, a man, or a group. And Mark alone says the rooster crowed twice. How do the accounts fit?
fit.short: Several people challenged Peter each time as he moved between door, fire and gateway. Mark notes two crowings; the others mention the decisive one.

events.title: The Council at Dawn
events.summary: At daybreak the whole council meets, questions Jesus again, condemns Him on His own words, and sends Him bound to Pilate.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark say the council questioned Jesus and condemned Him at night. Luke places the questioning at daybreak. Which is right?
fit.short: There were two sessions. Matthew and Mark tell the night hearing and mention the dawn meeting; Luke tells only the dawn meeting.

events.title: The End of Judas
events.summary: Seeing Jesus condemned, Judas returns the silver, confesses he betrayed innocent blood, and hangs himself; the priests buy a potter’s field, fulfilling prophecy.

fit.q: Matthew says Judas hanged himself and the priests bought the field. Acts says Judas bought a field and died by falling headlong and bursting open. How do these fit?
fit.short: Judas hanged himself, and his body later fell and burst open. The priests bought the field with his money, so it counted as his.

fit.q: Matthew says the prophecy was spoken by Jeremiah, but the words about thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter come from Zechariah 11:12–13. Did Matthew name the wrong prophet?
fit.short: Matthew blends Zechariah’s thirty pieces of silver with Jeremiah’s potter and field, and names Jeremiah, whose story supplies the field.

events.title: Before Pilate
events.summary: The council hands Jesus over to Pilate, the Roman governor, who questions Him privately about His kingship, finds no fault in Him, and marvels at His silence.

fit.q: Matthew, Mark and Luke give Jesus a brief answer, “It is as you say,” and then silence. John records a long conversation. Did Jesus speak to Pilate or not?
fit.short: Jesus spoke with Pilate privately inside (John) and was silent before His accusers outside (Matthew, Mark). “It is as you say” summarizes His answer.

events.title: Before Herod
events.summary: Pilate sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, who hopes to see a miracle; Jesus answers him nothing, and Herod mocks Him and sends Him back.

events.title: Pilate Hands Jesus Over
events.summary: Pilate tries again and again to release Jesus, but the crowd chooses Barabbas, the leaders press him, and Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified.

fit.q: John places the scourging in the middle of the trial, before “Behold the Man!” Matthew and Mark mention it after the crowd’s final choice, with the sentence. When was Jesus scourged?
fit.short: Matthew and Mark mention the scourging with the sentence; John shows when it happened. Or there were two beatings, a lighter and a heavier.

events.title: The Soldiers Mock Jesus
events.summary: Inside the Praetorium, Pilate’s soldiers dress Jesus as a mock king, crown Him with thorns, hail Him, strike Him and spit on Him.

fit.q: Was the robe scarlet (Matthew) or purple (Mark and John)?
fit.short: It was probably a soldier’s red cloak. Matthew names its color, scarlet; Mark and John name what it stood for, royal purple.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark tell of the mockery after Pilate’s sentence. John places the crown of thorns and the robe before Pilate shows Jesus to the crowd. When did it happen?
fit.short: The soldiers likely began mocking Jesus at His scourging (John) and renewed it with the whole garrison after the sentence (Matthew, Mark).

events.title: Simon Carries the Cross
events.summary: Jesus sets out for Golgotha carrying His cross; soldiers force Simon of Cyrene to carry it after Him, and Jesus warns the weeping women of Jerusalem.

fit.q: John says Jesus went out “bearing His cross.” Matthew, Mark and Luke say Simon of Cyrene carried it. Who carried the cross?
fit.short: Jesus set out carrying His cross (John); on the way the soldiers forced Simon to carry it for Him (Matthew, Mark, Luke).

events.title: The Crucifixion
events.summary: At Golgotha Jesus is crucified between two criminals under the title “The King of the Jews,” and, mocked by all, He prays for His executioners and promises Paradise.

fit.q: The four Gospels give the wording of the sign on the cross four different ways. What did it actually say?
fit.short: The sign was written in three languages, and each writer gives its essential charge: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.”

fit.q: Mark says Jesus was crucified at “the third hour,” about nine in the morning. John says Pilate was still giving his verdict at “about the sixth hour” (John 19:14), about noon. How can both be true?
fit.short: Hours were reckoned roughly, so late morning could fit both “third” and “about the sixth”; or John counted from midnight.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark say both robbers reviled Jesus. Luke says one mocked Him and the other defended Him. Which is it?
fit.short: Both robbers mocked at first; during the long hours on the cross one of them changed and turned to Jesus.

events.title: Darkness and the Death of Jesus
events.summary: From noon until three o’clock darkness covers the land; Jesus cries out to God, says, “It is finished,” commits His spirit to the Father and dies.

fit.q: Luke mentions the tearing of the temple veil before Jesus’ last cry. Matthew and Mark place it right after He breathed His last. When was it torn?
fit.short: Luke groups the two signs from heaven together; Matthew and Mark tie the tearing of the veil to the moment Jesus died.

events.title: The Veil Torn; the Centurion’s Confession
events.summary: As Jesus dies, the temple veil tears from top to bottom and a Roman centurion confesses Him; soldiers find Him already dead and pierce His side.

fit.q: Matthew and Mark record the centurion saying, “Truly this was the Son of God!” Luke has, “Certainly this was a righteous Man!” What did he say?
fit.short: The centurion likely said more than one thing; Luke highlights “righteous,” the last of many witnesses to Jesus’ innocence.

fit.q: John says Jesus’ mother and other women stood “by the cross” (John 19:25). Matthew, Mark and Luke say the women watched from a distance. Which is right?
fit.short: John describes the women near the cross earlier; the others describe them at a distance at the end, probably after Jesus’ mother had left.

events.title: The Burial of Jesus
events.summary: Joseph of Arimathea asks Pilate for Jesus’ body and, with Nicodemus, wraps it in linen and spices and lays it in a new tomb as the women watch.

fit.q: John says Joseph and Nicodemus bound Jesus’ body with about a hundred pounds of spices. Yet Luke says the women went home and prepared spices, and Mark says they bought spices after the Sabbath (Mark 16:1). Why more spices, and when were they made ready?
fit.short: The men’s burial was hurried before sunset; the women prepared spices Friday, bought more Saturday evening, and came to finish it.

events.title: The Tomb Sealed and Guarded
events.summary: The chief priests and Pharisees ask Pilate to secure Jesus’ tomb, then seal the stone and post a guard to stop any claim that He has risen.

events.title: The Earthquake and the Stone
events.summary: Early on the first day, an angel of the Lord rolls back the stone in a great earthquake and sits on it; the guards become like dead men.

fit.q: Matthew tells of the earthquake right after the women set out for the tomb (28:1). Mark and Luke say the women found the stone already rolled away. Did the women see the angel move it?
fit.short: Matthew never says the women saw the stone move; the guards witnessed it, and the women arrived to find it rolled away.

events.title: The Women Come to the Tomb
events.summary: Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and other women bring spices to Jesus’ tomb, find the great stone rolled away, and find no body inside.

fit.q: John says Mary Magdalene came “while it was still dark.” Mark says the women came “when the sun had risen.” When did they come?
fit.short: The women set out in the dark and arrived as the sun rose; John describes the start, Mark the arrival.

fit.q: Matthew names two women, Mark three, Luke a larger group, and John only Mary Magdalene. How many women came to the tomb?
fit.short: Several women came; each writer names some. Luke 24:10 lists three and “the other women,” and John follows Mary.

events.title: Mary Magdalene Runs to Tell Peter
events.summary: Finding the stone taken away, Mary Magdalene runs to Simon Peter and the disciple whom Jesus loved and tells them someone has taken the Lord from the tomb.

fit.q: In Matthew, Mark and Luke the women hear from angels that Jesus is risen. Here Mary tells Peter only that the body has been taken. Did she not hear the angels?
fit.short: Mary ran back as soon as she saw the open tomb, before the other women went in and heard the angels.

events.title: The Angels’ Message: “He Is Risen”
events.summary: Inside the empty tomb, angels tell the women not to be afraid: Jesus is not here; He is risen, as He said, and will meet His disciples in Galilee.

fit.q: Was there one angel (Matthew and Mark) or two (Luke)? Was he sitting (Mark), or were they standing (Luke)? And was the angel on the stone outside (Matthew) or inside the tomb (Mark)?
fit.short: Two angels were there; Matthew and Mark mention the one who spoke. Luke’s “stood” means appeared, and place and posture can change in a moment.

events.title: Peter and John at the Empty Tomb
events.summary: Hearing Mary’s report, Peter and the beloved disciple run to the tomb; they find the grave clothes left behind, and the other disciple sees and believes.

fit.q: Luke mentions only Peter running to the tomb. John says Peter and “the other disciple” went together. Did one man go, or two?
fit.short: Luke follows Peter, but Luke 24:24 says “certain of those who were with us went to the tomb.”

events.title: Jesus Appears to Mary Magdalene
events.summary: Weeping at the empty tomb, Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus, takes Him for the gardener, knows Him when He speaks her name, and is sent to His brethren.

fit.q: Mark says Jesus appeared “first to Mary Magdalene.” Matthew tells of Jesus meeting the women as they went to tell the disciples (Matthew 28:9; event 173). Who saw Him first?
fit.short: Mary, back at the tomb alone, saw Jesus first; the other women met Him afterward on their way to the disciples.

events.title: Jesus Meets the Women
events.place: On the way from the tomb
events.summary: As the women run from the empty tomb, the risen Jesus meets them, receives their worship, and sends word to His brethren to meet Him in Galilee.

fit.q: Matthew names Mary Magdalene among the women who came to the tomb, then says Jesus met “them” on the way. But John tells of Mary meeting Jesus alone in the garden, and Mark says He appeared “first to Mary Magdalene” (Mark 16:9). Was she with the women on the road?
fit.short: Mary Magdalene probably ran to Peter before the angel spoke, met Jesus alone at the tomb, and the other women met Him on their way.

events.title: The Guards’ Story
events.summary: Some of the guards report the empty tomb to the chief priests, who pay them a large sum to say the disciples stole Jesus’ body while they slept.

events.title: On the Road to Emmaus
events.summary: On Resurrection Sunday, Jesus joins two grieving disciples walking to Emmaus, explains from all the Scriptures why the Christ had to suffer, and is recognized as He breaks bread.

fit.q: Mark says the others did not believe the two from Emmaus. Luke says the others greeted them with “The Lord is risen indeed.” Did the disciples believe or not?
fit.short: Belief that evening was mixed. Luke himself says the group still doubted when Jesus appeared minutes later (Luke 24:37–41).

events.title: The Emmaus Disciples Return
events.summary: The two disciples hurry back from Emmaus to Jerusalem and find the eleven already saying that the Lord is risen and has appeared to Simon.

events.title: Jesus Appears to Peter
events.summary: On Resurrection Sunday the risen Jesus appears to Simon Peter, the disciple who had denied Him. Luke and Paul both record the meeting, but neither describes it.

events.title: Jesus Appears to the Disciples
events.summary: On Resurrection Sunday evening, Jesus stands among His frightened disciples, shows His wounds, eats before them, and sends them as the Father sent Him.

fit.q: Mark says Jesus appeared to “the eleven,” and Luke says the eleven were gathered. But John says Thomas was absent, so only ten apostles were there. Which is right?
fit.short: “The eleven” was the apostles’ group name after Judas, not an exact head count. Paul even calls them “the twelve.”

fit.q: On this evening Jesus breathes on the disciples and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Yet Luke records Him telling them to wait in Jerusalem for “the Promise of My Father,” which came at Pentecost (Luke 24:49; Acts 2). When did they receive the Spirit?
fit.short: Some see a real first gift of the Spirit that evening, with power poured out at Pentecost; others see an acted promise of Pentecost.

events.title: Jesus and Thomas
events.summary: A week after His resurrection Jesus appears again with Thomas present, offers him the proof he demanded, and Thomas confesses, “My Lord and my God!”

events.title: Breakfast by the Sea
events.summary: At the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus fills an empty net, gives His disciples breakfast, and restores Peter with three questions and a call to feed His sheep.

events.title: The Great Commission
events.summary: On a mountain in Galilee the risen Jesus claims all authority, sends His disciples to make disciples of all nations, and promises to be with them always.

fit.q: Matthew speaks of the eleven on the mountain in Galilee. Paul says Jesus was seen by more than five hundred at once. Were these the same appearance?
fit.short: Many think the five hundred gathered at this announced meeting in Galilee. Matthew names only the eleven, and Paul gives no place.

fit.q: In Mark, “Go into all the world” follows directly after Jesus appears to the eleven at the table (16:14–15), which sounds like Jerusalem on Resurrection Sunday. Matthew sets the commission on a mountain in Galilee. Which is it?
fit.short: Mark’s brief summary joins sayings without marking time. Jesus spoke of the mission several times, in Jerusalem and in Galilee.

events.title: Jesus Appears to James
events.summary: The risen Jesus appears to James, His brother, who had not believed in Him during His ministry. Paul records the meeting in a single line.

events.title: Last Instructions
events.summary: Over forty days the risen Jesus opens the Scriptures to His disciples, names them His witnesses, and tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the promised Spirit.

events.title: The Ascension
events.place: Near Bethany, the Mount of Olives
events.summary: Forty days after rising, Jesus leads His disciples out toward Bethany, blesses them with lifted hands, and is taken up into heaven, while angels promise He will return.

fit.q: Luke 24 moves from Resurrection Sunday to the ascension without a break, and Mark says Jesus was received up “after the Lord had spoken to them” (16:19). Yet Acts says He appeared to the disciples for forty days. Did the ascension happen on the day He rose?
fit.short: Luke wrote both accounts. His Gospel compresses the time; in Acts he states that Jesus appeared over forty days.
